learning_objective: 🎯 Discover why the Indian Constitution is like a living organism—how it adapts to changing times through amendments while keeping its core soul intact!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A constitution is not a dead rulebook. It is 'living' because it can change, evolve, and adapt to the new needs and aspirations of society over time, without collapsing.

The Indian Constitution is a blend. Some parts can be amended easily by a simple majority in Parliament (flexible). Other parts require a special majority, and some even require ratification by half the State legislatures (rigid).

An amendment bill can be introduced in either house of Parliament. For most major changes, it needs a 'Special Majority': majority of the total membership AND 2/3rd majority of members present and voting in both houses.

In the famous Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but it CANNOT destroy its 'Basic Structure' (like democracy, secularism, judicial independence).

The Constitution doesn't just change by formal amendments. The Supreme Court constantly interprets it in new ways (e.g., expanding the Right to Life to include the right to clean air), keeping it modern and alive.

fun_activity.title: 🏗️ The Jenga Tower of Laws
fun_activity.instructions: Think of the Constitution as a Jenga tower. You can move blocks around and add new ones on top (Amendments). But the 'Basic Structure' is the foundation blocks. If you remove them, the whole democracy collapses!

exam_tips: 📌 Memorize the three different ways the Constitution can be amended (simple majority, special majority, special majority + state ratification).
📌 The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) is the most important legal case in Indian constitutional history. Know its outcome perfectly.
📌 Explain *why* the constitution makers deliberately made it a mix of rigid and flexible.
quick_recap: ⭐ The Constitution has seen over 100 amendments, dealing with administrative, technical, and political changes.
⭐ The President has no veto power over constitutional amendment bills.
⭐ The Basic Structure doctrine acts as a shield against political majorities rewriting the core of the nation.
